newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German sick pay dispute heats up in regions.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German sick pay dispute heats up in regions.

text.p: The German dispute over a law cutting sick pay escalated on Friday as regional trade union committees and employer groups took it upon themselves to find a solution following Wednesday's collapse of national talks.

The Bavarian branch of the IG Metall metal and engineering trade union said after a meeting in the southern town of Regensburg that it would be cancelling existing wage contracts for the 650,000 workers in its region from January 31.

Such a move means the union can legally hold all-out strikes from the end of February. German engineering giants including Siemens AG and Bayerische Motorenwerke (BMW) have significant operations in Bavaria.

The decision follows the failure of talks between IG Metall negotiators and the Gesamtmetall employers group earlier this week to find a national agreement on how to cut labour costs in the sector within a 1997 wage round acceptable to the union.
The collapse of negotiations triggered wild-cat protests involving hundreds of thousands of metal workers around the country and resulting lost production at steel furnaces and car-assembly plants.
Employers in the steel-producing region of North-Rhine Westphalia, one of the areas worst hit by the protests, said on Friday they would now be taking the matter to an industrial court for a ruling.

The employers federation said it wanted to establish that the new law, which envisages a cut in sick payments from the current 100 percent of salary to 80 percent, could be applied to the 800,000 metal workers in North-Rhine Westphalia.
Large companies in the sector including Daimler-Benz AG earlier this month had to back down on attempts to enforce the law immediately after a first wave of protests.

While the industrial action has cost employers such as Daimler's Mercedes Benz vehicle unit hundreds of millions of marks in lost production, the IG Metall union has said such protests did not constitute strike action.
Under German law, workers can only hold full strikes after a six-week "peace duty" following the expiry of existing wage deals.

The Bavarian trade union committee, which represents around a fifth of the workers employed in the sector nationwide, is the first of the IG Metall regions to announce that it would be cancelling wage contracts.
IG Metall Bavarian regional head Werner Neugebauer said that although the decision did not mean it was gearing up for an "industrial struggle", it would not back down from such a fight if necessary.
